case_name: Sandor c. Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General Hospital
text:
Sandor c. Sir Mortimer B. Davis Jewish General
Hospital

2023 QCCS 2594

SUPERIOR COURT

Practice Division

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUÉBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTRÉAL

(Civil Division)

No :

500-17-113807-203

DATE :

July 12, 2023

______________________________________________________________________

BEFORE THE HONORABLE

ENRICO FORLINI, J.C.S.

______________________________________________________________________

PETER GEORGE SANDOR

c.

MARGIT SZABO SANDOR

Plaintiffs

c.

SIR MORTIMER B. DAVIS JEWISH
GENERAL HOSPITAL

Defendant

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

______________________________________________________________________

OVERVIEW

[
1
]

The Plaintiffs, who are husband and wife, claim $25,000,000 in
damages from the Jewish General
Hospital (“
Hospital
”) on the grounds that it misdiagnosed Mr. Sandor’s
mental health condition despite his numerous hospital visits and failed to
deliver adequate care to him.

[
2
]

Plaintiffs are unrepresented litigants.

[
3
]

Plaintiffs failed to set down the case for trial before the expiry
of the strict time limit of article 173 of the
Code of Civil Procedure

(“
C.C.P.
”

or “
Code
”).

[
4
]

As a result, they ask the court to grant them relief from the
consequences of their failure to do so, i.e., that they are presumed to have
discontinued their originating application.

[
5
]

The Hospital contests the application for relief on the grounds that
the Plaintiffs have failed to prove that they were under an impossibility to
act

within the strict time limit. If the court
concludes that they have, it argues that the court should nonetheless exercise
its discretion and refuse to grant them relief because they have not met the
criteria set forth by the Court of Appeal in
Zodiac
.

[
6
]

The Court must therefore determine whether to grant Plaintiffs relief
under article 177 of the
Code
.

ANALYSIS

1.

Legal Framework

[
7
]

According to article 173
C.C.P
., a plaintiff must file a
request with the court to have the case set down for trial and judgement within
a strict time limit of 6 months, the starting point of the delay varying
according to circumstances.

[
8
]

A plaintiff who fails to do so is presumed to have discontinued
his/her action pursuant to article 177 par. 1
C.C.P
.

[
9
]

However, article 177 par. 2
C.C.P
. affords the plaintiff the
possibility of being relieved from his/her failure to set down the case if the
court “is satisfied that it was impossible in fact for [the plaintiff] to act
within the time limit. In such an instance, the court modifies the case
protocol and sets a new time limit, which cannot be extended except for
compelling reasons.”

[
10
]

The case law is well settled that a court must
apply a two-step framework to determine whether it will grant relief to a
plaintiff who has failed to file a request for setting down within the strict
time limit.
[1]

[
11
]

At the first step, the court must be satisfied
that the applicant meets the precondition that it has demonstrated its impossibility
to act within the prescribed time limit.
[2]

[
12
]

At the second step, the court exercises its
discretionary power to decide whether to relieve the requesting party of the
consequences of its delay. Although this is a discretionary power, it must be
exercised judicially, that is, following the relevant considerations.
[3]

[
13
]

The principal considerations relevant to the
exercise of judicial discretion under paragraph 2 of article 177
C.C.P
.
are
[4]
:

13.1.

the harm that will result from the decision to
refuse to grant relief;

13.2.

the apparent seriousness of the claim;

13.3.

the time that has elapsed since the expiration
of the time limit; and

13.4.

the conduct of the parties or their lawyers with
respect to the conduct of the proceeding.

2.

Application to This Case - Should the Plaintiffs Be Relieved of the
Consequences Set Out In Article 177 C.C.P?

[
14
]

Applying the two-step legal framework, the Court
must first determine whether the Plaintiffs have proven that it was impossible
in fact for them to act within the time limit prescribed by article 173 C.C.P.

[
15
]

In the event that this has been established, the
Court must then exercise its discretion to decide whether to relieve the
Plaintiffs of the consequence imposed by article 177
C.C.P.

2.1.

Have the Plaintiffs Proven That it was Impossible for Them to Act?

[
16
]

The Plaintiffs had the obligation to file a request to have the case set down
for trial and judgement before December 15, 2022.

[
17
]

Plaintiffs argue that it was impossible for them
to set down the case for trial before the expiry of this deadline because on
December 1, 2022, the Hospital filed an application to dismiss their claim
under article 51
C.C.P.
, application which was presentable on December 15.
They believed that the issue of the delay to set the case down for trial would
be addressed at the hearing of the application to dismiss, but a hearing never
took place because the application was decided and dismissed on the face of the
record.

[
18
]

They only learned on December 28, 2022 that a
judgement was rendered on December 20 dismissing the Hospital’s application to
dismiss and they acted promptly after that to seek relief.

[
19
]

The Hospital argues that this is the second time
that the Plaintiffs have failed to set down the case for trial within the
strict time limit of article 173
C.C.P
. Moreover, they were present at
court on August 26, 2022, when the time limit to set down the case for trial
was extended to December 15, 2022 and were thus well aware that they had to act
before the expiry of this deadline. It adds that the Plaintiffs failed to set down the case for trial because of
their negligence and their ignorance of the procedural rules, which does not
qualify as an impossibility to act.

[
20
]

Impossibility to act is a question of fact. The
burden of proving impossibility lies with the plaintiff.
[5]

[
21
]

Impossibility
to act is a relative
impossibility
, not an absolute one. It does not require the person invoking it to
demonstrate that he or she was prevented from acting by an invincible obstacle
beyond his or her control.
[6]
I
t will suffice for the
party to show
a de facto,
relative impossibility. A
plaintiff’s burden in this regard is not very demanding.
[7]
That said, the evidence must
nonetheless be sufficiently clear and convincing.

[
22
]

Impossibility
in fact to act will exist if the party, whether she/he was
represented by a lawyer or not, acted diligently. Conversely,
impossibility
to act won’t be found to exist where the plaintiff was
not diligent or could have remedied the effects of
an omission but abstained from doing so because of his negligence. Diligence is
a
sine qua non
precondition of
impossibility
in fact to act.
[8]

[
23
]

The fact that Plaintiffs are not represented by
a lawyer and that they may be unfamiliar with the rules of civil procedure is
no excuse.

[
24
]

A person who takes legal action without the
assistance of a member of the Bar runs the risk of making a mistake, but as
article 23 of the
Code
explicitly states, the fact remains that he or
she has the same obligations as a party who is represented by a lawyer and
incurs the same penalties if he or she fails to abide by the rules set forth in
the
Code.
[9]

[
25
]

The legislator enacted article 173 and following
of the
Code
to ensure the rapid progress of proceedings, and a person
acting without a lawyer is not exempt from complying with these provisions, nor
from being aware of them.
[10]

[
26
]

The fact that the Plaintiffs are self-represented
litigants is a factor that the Court must consider in its analysis of the issue
of their impossibility to act.

[
27
]

It is true that ignorance of the law does not
constitute grounds for failure to comply with the time limit in article 173
C.C.P.

[
28
]

But this principle must be tempered by two
others. Firstly, judges owe a duty to provide assistance to un-represented
litigants, the scope of which varies and is determined by the case law.
[11]

[
29
]

Secondly, judges also have an obligation to
ensure and promote access to justice. This principle is enshrined in the
Preliminary Provision of the
Code of Civil Procedure
.

[
30
]

It is also proclaimed in the
Statement of
Principles on Self-represented Litigants and Accused Persons
adopted by the
Canadian Judicial Council.
[12]

[
31
]

The
Statement of Principles on
Self-represented Litigants
notably states:

A.

PROMOTING RIGHTS OF ACCESS

STATEMENT: Judges, the courts and other
participants in the justice system have a responsibility to promote
opportunities for all persons to understand and meaningfully present their
case, regardless of representation.

PRINCIPLES:

1.

Access to
justice for self-represented persons requires all aspects of the court process
to be, as much as possible, open, transparent, clearly defined, simple,
convenient and accommodating.

…

B.
PROMOTING EQUAL JUSTICE

STATEMENT: Judges, the courts and other
participants in the justice system have a responsibility to promote access to
the justice system for all persons on an equal basis, regardless of
representation.

PRINCIPLES:

1.

Judges

and

court

administrators

should

do

whatever

is

possible

to

provide

a

fair

and

impartial

process

and

prevent

an

unfair

disadvantage

to

self-represented

persons.

2.

Self-represented

persons

should

not

be

denied

relief

on

the

basis

of

a

minor

or

easily

rectified

deficiency

in

their

case.

[
32
]

While

there
are not two sets of court rules – one
for persons who are represented by lawyers and one for persons who
are not, the
Code

of Civil Procedure
must nonetheless be
interpreted and applied in a manner that is consistent with promoting access to
justice, keeping in mind that judges must at all times maintain and preserve
their duty of impartiality.

[
33
]

In the instant case, the Plaintiffs argue that
when they received on December 1, 2022, notification of the Hospital’s application
to dismiss (art. 51
C.C.P.
), they were under the impression that they
would be called to a hearing on this application and that the judge who would
hear the application would raise the issue of extending the deadline to set the
case down for trial. They expected to address the issue of the article 173
C.C.P
.
deadline at this hearing.

[
34
]

However, no hearing ever took place for the
Hospital’s application to dismiss since the Court decided to rule on it on the
face of the record.

[
35
]

On December 20, 2022, the Court issued its
judgment and dismissed the Hospital’s application to dismiss.

[
36
]

The Plaintiffs were not made aware of this
judgment until they received it from the Hospital’s lawyers on December 28,
2022.

[
37
]

In fact, the December 20, 2022, judgment is
still not entered in the court register (
plumitif
) and the Plaintiffs
never received a notice of judgment as is required by article 335
C.C.P
.

[
38
]

The Plaintiffs’ state of confusion or
uncertainty with respect to their obligation to set the case down for trial
during the period from December 1 to December 28, 2022, is understandable.

[
39
]

Their failure to act does not result from their
negligence but rather from circumstances that from a lay person’s point of
view, and even a lawyer for that matter, could be seen as not clearly defined.
This is not a case where the plaintiffs acted negligently.

[
40
]

If a hearing had taken place on December 15,
2022 as announced in the notice of presentation accompanying the application to
dismiss, the Court believes that the issue of extending the delay to set down
the case for trail would have been raised, either by one of the parties, or by
the judge presiding this hearing, in performing his duty to provide assistance and promoting access to justice.

[
41
]

This case is distinguishable from the recent
Court of Appeal decision in
Gauthier v. Procureur général du Québec

which the Hospital relies on.
[13]

[
42
]

In
Gauthier
, the Court of Appeal held
that Mr. Gauthier’s lack of follow-up of his file with his lawyer during a
one-year period constituted lack of diligence and precluded a finding of
impossibility to act.
[14]

The Court of Appeal did not find compelling Mr. Gauthier’s argument, that the
lack of communication stemmed from an erroneous e-mail address.

[
43
]

In the instant case, the Court does not find
that the Plaintiffs inaction between December 1 and December 15, 2022, was
caused their negligence. Quite the contrary, the Court finds that they were
diligent and had compelling reasons for missing the December 15 deadline.

[
44
]

The Court finds that the Plaintiffs have proven
that it was impossible for them to act within the time December 15 time limit and that they had compelling
reasons for missing the deadline.
[15]

2.2.

Should the Plaintiffs be relieved of the consequence set out in art.
177
C.C.P.
?

[
45
]

While the Court has concluded that the
Plaintiffs have met their burden of proof at the first step of the two-step
framework, it must now exercise its discretion and decide whether to relieve the Plaintiffs of the
consequences of their delay, weighing the four criteria identified in
Zodiac
.

2.2.1.

The Harm That Will Result from the Decision
to Refuse to Grant Plaintiffs Relief

[
46
]

If the Plaintiffs’ application to obtain relief
is refused, they are presumed to have discontinued their originating
application. This presumed discontinuance has two main consequences.

[
47
]

Firstly, in accordance with article 213
C.C.P
.,
the plaintiffs must pay the Hospital the costs incurred by its claim. While
this is a prejudice, it is of little importance and its significance is
relatively minor in the exercise of the Court’s discretion.

[
48
]

Secondly, the deemed discontinuance leads to the
application of
article 2894
of the
Civil Code of Québec
(“
C.C.Q
.
”),
which provides that the interruption of prescription of a right of action that
results from the filing of an originating application does not occur if the demand
is discontinued. Thus, if a new originating application cannot be filed within
the prescription period, the party who is not relieved of the consequences of
his default risks irretrievably forfeiting his or her right of action.

[
49
]

In the instant case, according to the
allegations contained in the modified originating application, the faults that
the Plaintiffs complain of occurred between 2011 and 2016
[16]
. Moreover, the Plaintiffs
allege that Mr. Sandor only got the proper treatment from another hospital in
2017-2018.

[
50
]

Given these allegations, there is a not
insignificant risk that Plaintiffs’ claim might be prescribed if they are not
granted relief under article 177
C.C.P
.

[
51
]

In fact, the Hospital has already raised this as
a ground of defense and will undoubtedly raise it anew should the Plaintiffs be
required to file a new originating application if their application for relief
is not granted.

[
52
]

This criterion militates in favour of granting the
application to be relieved of failure to set down the case.

2.2.2.

The Apparent Seriousness of the
Plaintiffs’ Claim

[
53
]

The Hospital invites the Court to conclude that
the Plaintiffs’ claim is manifestly ill-founded.

[
54
]

However, as the Court of Appeal stated in
Heaslip
v. McDonald
, caution must be exercised before concluding at the stage of an
application under article 177
C.C.P.
that an action is not sufficiently
serious.
[17]

[
55
]

Applying this rule to the present case, the Court
is not of the opinion that the Plaintiffs’ claim is manifestly ill-founded.

[
56
]

The Hospital has attempted on two occasions to obtain
the preliminary dismissal of the Plaintiffs’ originating application and each
time it has failed.

[
57
]

In July 2021, the Hospital filed an application
for dismissal on the grounds that the originating application was unfounded in
law even if the facts alleged are true (art. 168 (2)
C.C.P.
).

[
58
]

By judgement dated October 5, 2021, the Court
dismissed the Hospital’s application to dismiss in so far as it concerns the
Plaintiffs George Sandor and his wife Margit Szabo. Only those portions of the
claim in which the Plaintiffs purported to claim damages on behalf of their
children was dismissed
[18]
.

[
59
]

On December 1, 2022, after having examined on
discovery Mr. Sandor, the Hospital brought an application to dismiss based on
article 51
C.C.P
. on the grounds that the claim is clearly unfounded,
frivolous, and abusive considering that it is prescribed, the faults are
unfounded in fact and in law, and the damages claimed are abusive and non
causal.

[
60
]

By judgment dated December 20, 2022, the Court,
on the face of the record and without a hearing, dismissed the Hospital’s
application under article 51 C.C.P.

[
61
]

Two judges of this Court have reviewed the
Hospital’s arguments seeking preliminary dismissal of the Plaintiffs’ claim and
both decided that dismissal prior to the trial on the merits was not warranted.

[
62
]

While the Hospital raises compelling arguments
in support of its defense, considering that at this stage the Court must act
with caution, it cannot conclude that the Plaintiffs’ claim is manifestly ill
founded. They are entitled to their day in Court.

2.2.3.

The Time That Has Elapsed Since the Expiration
of the Time Limit

[
63
]

The length of time elapsed since the expiry of
the delay to file a request to set the case down for trial is a relevant
consideration. As the Court of Appeal writes in
Zodiac
, a short delay of
one day does not have the same impact as a delay of one year. The longer the
delay, the greater the burden on the applicant. In all cases, the elapsed time
must be justified.
[19]

[
64
]

Two periods must be taken into account. The
first is the period between the deadline for setting down for trial and
judgement and the time when the plaintiff or his lawyer discovers that the
deadline has been missed. The second period corresponds to the time between the
date on which the plaintiff discovers that the deadline has been missed and the
date on which the application to be relieved of the failure to set down the
case for trial is filed.
[20]

[
65
]

This first period may be justified if its
duration is compatible with the alleged error.

[
66
]

This second period must be very short, as both
the party asking to be relieved, and when the party is represented, his lawyer,
have a duty to react promptly as soon as they become aware of the delay.

[
67
]

In the instant case the deadline under article
173
C.C.P.
was December 15, 2022.

[
68
]

The Plaintiffs are informed on December 28,
2022, when they receive from the Hospital’s lawyer a copy of the December 20,
2022 judgement dismissing the Hospital’s application to dismiss under article
51
C.C.P
., that they omitted to have the case set down for trial before
the expiry of the deadline.
[21]

[
69
]

Thirteen days pass between the expiry of the
delay under article 173
C.C.P
.  and the day they discovered their
failure to set the case down for trial.

[
70
]

This is a short period and is justified as it is
compatible with their alleged error.

[
71
]

The Plaintiffs’ application to be relieved of
the default is dated February 21, 2023. It is notified by email to the Hospital
on March 3 and filed with the court office on March 6, 2023.
[22]

[
72
]

There is a 65-day delay between the date on
which the Plaintiffs discover that they have missed the deadline and the date
on which their application is notified to the Hospital.

[
73
]

The Plaintiffs explain that when they first learn
that they failed to set down the case for trial, it was the Christmas holiday
period. Many of the lawyers they tried to contact to obtain assistance and advice
were on vacation or otherwise out of the office.

[
74
]

Ultimately, after the Christmas holidays, the
Plaintiffs were able to obtain the assistance of a lawyer and obtain the advice
and information they needed to be able to file the application for relief.

[
75
]

In assessing the reasonableness of the delay
taken by the Plaintiffs to file their application, the Court must take into
account their level of knowledge or familiarity with the legal system and the
way cases progress with the courts.
[23]

[
76
]

While the present lawsuit filed against the
Hospital is not the Plaintiffs’ first foray in the Québec legal system, there
is no evidence that shows that the Plaintiffs have anything beyond a very basic
or minimal knowledge of the functioning of the Québec legal system.

[
77
]

Considering all the circumstances, the Court
does not believe that the Plaintiffs failed to act promptly. For example, in
Villeneuve
v. Langlois Avocats
, the Court of Appeal held that a delay of 131 days
between the expiry of the delay to set the case down for trial and the filing
of the application to be relieved was a short delay.
[24]

[
78
]

This criterion also militates in favour of
granting Plaintiffs relief.

2.2.4.

The Conduct of the Parties with Respect to
the Conduct of the Proceeding
.

[
79
]

This criterion concerns the conduct of both the
parties and their lawyer (when the party is represented) regarding the conduct
of the proceedings.

[
80
]

The
Zodiac
case distinguishes between two
types of behaviour: gross negligence, general disorganization, or carelessness
with regard to the conduct of the proceedings or the management of the file
versus errors in good faith in the normal course of the practice of law, errors
which may be the result from negligence or even gross negligence.
[25]

[
81
]

Where the conduct of the applicant and its
lawyer does not reveal gross negligence, general disorganization, or
carelessness regarding the conduct of the proceedings, the application could be
granted, subject to all the other relevant criteria set out in
Zodiac
. In
other words, behaviour that is akin to an error in good fait should militate in
favor of granting the application to be relieved of default.
[26]

[
82
]

The Hospital argues that the Plaintiffs behavior
throughout the proceeding shows a lack of regard for the rules of procedure and
a lack of diligence.

[
83
]

The Court does not believe that the Plaintiffs’
behavior qualifies as one of gross negligence or carelessness with regards to
the conduct of proceedings.

[
84
]

Rather, their failure to respect the deadline to
set down the case for trial stems from an error made in good faith. This error
results from their misunderstanding of the effects of the filing of the
Hospital’s application to dismiss had on the computation of the delay under
article 173
C.C.P
. This error may constitute negligence, but it does not
constitute gross negligence or carelessness with regard to the conduct of the
proceedings.

[
85
]

It is an error that even a lawyer may have
committed.

[
86
]

This criterion militates in favor of granting
the Plaintiffs’ relief.

2.3.

Conclusion

[
87
]

The Court concludes that the Plaintiffs must be relieved
of the consequence set out in article 177
C.C.P
. Firstly, they have
discharged the burden of proving that it was impossible in fact for them to act
within the December 15, 2022, time limit. Secondly, applying the four criteria
identified in
Zodiac,
the Court considers that it should exercise its
discretion and that it is in the interest of justice to relieve the Plaintiffs
of the consequences of their failure to act.

3.

Case Management Measure

[
88
]

When a court grants a plaintiff relief under
article 177 of the
Code
, paragraph 2 states that “[i]n such an instance,
the court modifies the case protocol and sets a new time limit, which cannot be
extended except for compelling reasons.

[
89
]

In the present case, despite the fact that the
originating application was filed in September 2020, the parties have not yet
been able to establish a case protocol and to file it with the court office.

[
90
]

Accordingly, the Court will order the parties to
collaborate in establishing a case protocol, and to file it with the court
office within 15 days from the date of this judgement.

[
91
]

If a party fails to co-operate in
establishing the case protocol, then the rule set forth in article 152
C.C.P
.
will apply. If both parties
file a proposed case protocol within the time limit for filing and cannot agree
concerning the content of the protocol, the Court will order

the
parties to participate in a case management conference.

FOR THESE
REASONS, THE COURT:

[
92
]

GRANTS

Plaintiffs’ Application to be Relieved of the Default and for Time Limit
Extension;

[
93
]

RELIEVES
the
Plaintiffs of their failure to file with the court office their
request to set down the case for trial and judgement

and of the consequences of their failure to file this request;

[
94
]

EXTENDS
the time
limit to file the request to set down the case for trial and judgement to
October 1, 2023;

[
95
]

ORDERS
the
parties to collaborate in establishing a case protocol, and to file it with the
court office within fifteen (15) days from the date of this judgement,
FAILING
WHICH
, each party must file a proposed case protocol within the time limit
for filing. On the expiry of a period of 10 days after the date of the filing,
the proposed case protocol serves as the case protocol filed on that same date,
unless the party that failed to co-operate has filed a notice stating the
points on which the parties differ. If both parties have filed a proposed case
protocol within the time limit for filing and cannot agree concerning the
content of the protocol, or if one of the parties’ files a notice stating the
points on which the parties differ, the Court
ORDERS
the
parties to participate in a case management conference and to notify to the
other party a notice of case management within ten (10) days from the expiry of
the fifteen (15) time limit to file;

[
96
]

WITHOUT COSTS.

Williams v. Valeurs
mobilières Desjardins
inc.,
2019 QCCA 1842
